hook_text: June 1913: families on the winter roads with dying cattle. A new law said they could no longer rent the land they farmed.
clip_script: In 1913 the Union passed the Natives Land Act. Africans, about two-thirds of the people, could now own or rent land in only about seven per cent of the country. Sharecroppers were told: become farm servants, or go. Thousands went, in the cold, with their cattle. Sol Plaatje called it becoming an outcast in the land of your birth. The same year, Indian South Africans said: enough. A three-pound tax, marriages not recognised, borders they could not cross. Gandhi's answer was truth-force. Women crossed without permits. Miners struck. Two thousand people marched into the Transvaal. In 1914 the tax was gone. The Land Act stayed.
visual_style: A whiteboard split screen: on one side a map with a small shaded seven per cent and a family walking with cattle; on the other, a line of marchers crossing a border at Volksrust.
pacing: Measured for the Land Act, rising with the march, ending on the contrast.
